Dear Sion Buckler

In order to proceed with your request we require some further information:


  *   Please provide the title number in which you require this information for

You may need to apply for a Search of the Index Map to find out if a specific property or area of land is registered and, if it is, the title number(s) of that land. Further information on this service is provided below.

Once you have sufficiently clarified the relevant land in which you would like this information for, we will proceed with your request.

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware the information you have requested is held within our registers that are open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we are unable to provide access to this information via an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) or a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request and it is likely a refusal notice will be issued for this information.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:
www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Their contact details are as follows:

English language phone [phone redacted]
Welsh language phone [phone redacted]

Telephone lines are open between 08:00 and 17:00 Monday to Friday This does not include Bank Holidays.
Website: www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

What is the Index Map?
HM Land Registry keeps a computerised 'index map' based on the Ordnance Survey map. This computerised map provides an index of the land in every registered title and pending application for first registration.

Applying for an Index Map Search
You apply for an official search of the index map using form SIM<https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/index-map-application-for-an-official-search-sim>.
This will need to be printed, completed and sent to our Standard address<https://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-address-for-applications#standard-addresses>.

  *        be drawn to scale
  *        be based on the current large scale Ordnance Survey map
  *        indicate scale and north point
  *        show property extent with suitable colouring and position in relation to nearby roads and other features plans of flats and maisonettes
     indicate floor level (if any) of the property.
  *
You can also search by map on our Search for land and property information<https://www.gov.uk/search-property-information-land-registry> service.

Yours sincerely

> Dear Mr. Gale,
>
> Thank you again for your helpful reply and for viewing the original
> Manorial Documents Committee returns (HMC9/311). I entirely understand that
> it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful
> for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW
> catalogue.
>
> To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to
> within the family as the *“Williams Title”* (or the equitable interest
> conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period *c. 1900–1915*. It
> arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House
> Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry
> operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted
> permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title
> / permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas
> is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute
> Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along
> with its index card in 1984).
>
> This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute
> estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural
> tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which
> Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted
> successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876
> limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial
> quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern
> title dispute.
>
> *Why this matters now* The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (*BP Properties
> Ltd v Buckler*) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence
> letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams
> (née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing
> her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of
> the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As
> the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational
> misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders,
> licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her
> heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and
> demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for
> which reparations are now sought.
>
> To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive
> timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that
> highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period.
> With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus
> searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916
> leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas
> references).
>
> I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise
> sub-series or box references within those collections that cover
> Llandough manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving
> index cards, rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams /
> Daniel Thomas in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.
>
> Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your
> further assistance.
>
> Kind regards
>
> Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and additional information explaining the background to your enquiry.

Unfortunately, apart from the pre-war survey returns The National Archives has only the only information recorded on-line MDR, and the following entry appears most pertinent to your enquiry held at the Glamorgan Archives: court book, with other manors D/D B M/3  for 1884-1937 held at Glamorgan Archives. We do not hold any other finding manorial finding aids such as old index cards as the entries were updated in 1990’s summarising the archive services catalogues of the time. Also, I have no more access or information relating to the various archive collections held outside of The National Archives than any other researcher. The Bute Estate Archives held at the Glamorgan Archive Service are catalogued under collection reference DB: Bute, Glamorgan Estate 

The only physical source we hold is a paper copy of the catalogue of 370 pages of the ‘Stuart family, Marquesses of Bute Archives: manorial records and estate papers, mainly rel to Glamorgan and Monmouthshire estates’ deposited at the National Library of Wales (NLW) in July 1950 (Ref. NRA 581) which submitted to the National of Register of Archives which now has a summarised entry in our on-line catalogue Discovery: Glamorganshire (Cardiff, Llantrisant, etc) and Monmouthshire (Newport, Machen, etc, NRA Stuart 581  The reference to the Manors of Leckwith, Llandough, Cogan Cosmeston and Walterson is M17, pages 113-116 of the catalogue although most of the material predates 1900. This can be viewed at the library reading room at The National Archive by prior appointment. The Bute Estate archives for Glamorgan appear to be held at the National Library of Wales and the Glamorgan Archive Service. The NLW paper catalogue (Ref. NRA 581) broadly mirrors the NLW on-line catalogue: Bute Estate Records, - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts 

A possibility worth bearing in mind is that the property, Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin may ceased to have been held by copyhold tenure by 1900 and instead may have been held instead by a leasehold tenancy which if this was the case the manorial records will not be relevant to your research. As you mentioned the Bute estate interests were steadily disposed of from c1900 culminating in sale of the estate’s leasehold interest to the Western Ground Rents Company in 1938. This led to the widespread dispersal and possibly destruction of the Bute estate records which makes it particularly challenging to track down and identify individual documents. Furthermore, catalogues often include bundle lists with individual documents concealed by a general description of the contents of the whole bundle.

I regret I cannot be of any further assistance; however I hope your further research proves fruitful.

Kind regards

Dear Mr. Gale,

Thank you again for your helpful reply and for viewing the original Manorial Documents Committee returns (HMC9/311). I entirely understand that it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW catalogue.

To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to within the family as the “Williams Title” (or the equitable interest conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period c. 1900–1915. It arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title / permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along with its index card in 1984).

This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876 limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern title dispute.

Why this matters now The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (BP Properties Ltd v Buckler) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams (née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders, licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for which reparations are now sought.

To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period. With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916 leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas references).

I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise sub-series or box references within those collections that cover Llandough manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving index cards, rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams / Daniel Thomas in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.

Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your further assistance.

Kind regards

Sion Buckler

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT



Dear Sir/Madam,



This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.



This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.



My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.



I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.



The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.



The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:



1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.

2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.



These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.



In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.



This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:



*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).

*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:



*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.

*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.

*       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.

*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.

*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).

*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).

*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).

*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.



These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Dear Mr. Gale,

Thank you again for your helpful reply and for viewing the original
Manorial Documents Committee returns (HMC9/311). I entirely understand that
it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful
for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW
catalogue.

To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to
within the family as the *“Williams Title”* (or the equitable interest
conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period *c. 1900–1915*. It
arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House
Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry
operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted
permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title
/ permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas
is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute
Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along
with its index card in 1984).

This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute
estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural
tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which
Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted
successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876
limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial
quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern
title dispute.

*Why this matters now* The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (*BP Properties
Ltd v Buckler*) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence
letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams
(née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing
her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of
the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As
the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational
misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders,
licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her
heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and
demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for
which reparations are now sought.

To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive
timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that
highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period.
With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus
searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916
leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas
references).

I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise
sub-series or box references within those collections that cover Llandough
manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving index cards,
rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams / Daniel Thomas
in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.

Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your
further assistance.

Kind regards

Sion Buckler

Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.



The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.



The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.



These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.



In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. *       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.

Dear Sion,

Thank you for your email regarding Great House Farm, Llandough. However, I must inform you that much of the content in your correspondence falls outside the scope of Cadw’s work.

In relation to the claim of 'archaeological suppression' involving the discovery of a Roman soldier in full armour in 1888, any such find would typically have been reported in the antiquarian press at either the national or local level. It is possible that records of this nature may be held by local museums. It is worth noting that the first Ancient Monuments Act was passed in 1882, focusing solely on bringing threatened ancient monuments into guardianship. The legal recognition of nationally important archaeology did not come about until the Ancient Monuments Consolidation and Amendment Act of 1913.

Upon reviewing the Cof Cymru database, I found that there are no designated historic assets relevant to this topic. However, Archwilio contains two records that document the involvement of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT):

1. Great House Farm HER site entry - GGAT03586s
2. Land at Great House Farm HER event entry - GGATE003872, which includes GGAT's 1990 archaeological assessment report commissioned by BP Properties Ltd.

Any advice or correspondence that Cadw may have provided should be preserved in the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW) National Monuments Record of Wales (NMRW). I recommend you contact the NMRW to access any relevant documents. Additionally, you may want to reach out to Heneb and the Vale of Glamorgan Local Planning Authority (LPA) to explore what records they might hold concerning this matter.

Kind regards,

Jenna Arnold

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and for clarifying the subject of your enquiry.

As you know the Manorial Documents Register (MDR) only gives general descriptions of the content, extent and location of the manorial records recorded in the register: LLANDOUGH MANOR | The National Archives  The manorial records for the Manor of Llandough are held at the National Library of Wales, Glamorgan Archives and West Glamorgan Archives, and their catalogues can be accessed on-line : NLW Catalogue  , Glamorgan Archives Catalogue  and Archive Collections - Swansea 

The Welsh entries in the online MDR were added in the 1990’s were based on the survey returns to the Manorial Documents Committee received from institutions and private owners during the 1920’s. These were subsequently passed to the custody of the Historical Manuscripts Commission in 1959 which amalgamated with the Public Record Office to form The National Archives in 2003. I have requested to see the original returns for Manor of Llandough to see if they can provide any additional information on the documentation relating to the manor (Ref. HMC 9/311: https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C5879336 )

There are several other manors with a similar name in Glamorgan and a MDR search using the search term “Llandough” gives the following result: Search results: Llandough Glamorgan | The National Archives    Sometimes the administration of different manors were brought together and this appears to have occurred  with the Llandough and St May’s Church Manors : https://archives.library.wales/index.php/manors-of-llandough-and-st-mary-church

I will contact you again once I have had an opportunity to look at the original returns sent to Manorial Documents Committee. I hope this preliminary information is of assistance.

Yours sincerely

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.



My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.



The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.



The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:



1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.

2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.



These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.



In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.



This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:



*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).

*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).

*       Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.



Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.



Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:



*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.

In that context, I am not seeking to pay for copies of records whose accuracy is itself in question, nor to participate financially in processes that may inadvertently perpetuate errors arising from that period. My intention is to place relevant public bodies on notice of a potential issue of public record integrity and heritage governance, not to obtain documents for private interest. I have written to the Senedd calling for a public enquiry too. I've notified the land registry and serious fraud teams too.

I am therefore asking that my correspondence be treated as a formal expression of concern regarding the reliability and completeness of the archival record as it relates to this site, and that this concern be noted accordingly. I would also be grateful if you could advise which department or officer is appropriate for addressing concerns of this nature, where the issue is not access but potential historical misrepresentation within public records.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging any impropriety on the part of current archive staff. My concern relates to historical processes and decisions, and to ensuring that those matters are properly examined rather than inadvertently reinforced.

Dear Mr Buckler.

Thank you for your email.

Glamorgan Archives had at one time a large number of paper catalogues, along with card indexes.  The data from these was transferred into our catalogue when we moved from analogue to digital.  The original catalogues and cards were not retained.

Our catalogue only records descriptions of documents that are held within our collection.  If a document is permanently withdrawn from the collection, we would remove the description from the catalogue. Many of our records are private records held on deposit on behalf of the owner.  We have no control over what they do or don’t give us.  The owner retains the right to withdraw these documents if they wish.

Yours sincerely,

Rhian Diggins [cid:image001.jpg@01DCA247.5A36F0C0]

I have written to the Senedd calling for a public enquiry too. I've notified the land registry and serious fraud teams too.

I am therefore asking that my correspondence be treated as a formal expression of concern regarding the reliability and completeness of the archival record as it relates to this site, and that this concern be noted accordingly. I would also be grateful if you could advise which department or officer is appropriate for addressing concerns of this nature, where the issue is not access but potential historical misrepresentation within public records.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging any impropriety on the part of current archive staff. My concern relates to historical processes and decisions, and to ensuring that those matters are properly examined rather than inadvertently reinforced.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Mr Gale,

Thank you for your reply of 12 February. I would like to clarify and narrow
my request to ensure there is no misunderstanding regarding the records I
am trying to locate.

My correspondence is *not* seeking an adjudication of ownership or title —
I fully accept the stated remit boundaries of the Manorial Documents
Register (MDR). Rather, my enquiry concerns the existence of *any archival
reference, index card, catalogue entry, or pointer to a document
historically known as the “Williams Title”*, which was, according to
contemporaneous family testimony, at one point:

   1.

   Held in the *local public library* in the first half of the twentieth
   century; and
   2.

   Indexed in some manner (e.g., an index card or catalogue reference) that
   persisted even after the original document could not be located.

My understanding of the MDR — as described on your own website — is that it
exists to provide brief descriptions of manorial records and details of
their locations:

“An official index of English and Welsh manorial records providing brief
descriptions of documents and details of their locations… It does *not*
include title deeds or conveyances, and is *not* a register of ownership of
manorial lordships or rights.”
https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search
<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/manor-search?utm_source=chatgpt.com>

Based on that description, I would be grateful if you could confirm whether:

   1.

   *Any catalogue entries, index cards, reference pointers, or archival
   descriptions* relating to the *Manor of Llandough* or the *Williams
   family title* exist in the MDR or related archival catalogues.
   2.

   If so, the *reference identifiers* and information on how these can be
   consulted in person or via digitised records.

To be precise, I am looking for historical references to the *index card or
listing* for the Williams Title — whether held in a library, local record
office, or other institutional archive — rather than a claim for ownership
judgment itself.

If such a reference does not currently appear in the MDR, I would greatly
appreciate guidance on where any known catalogue cards or entry lists for
manorial documents from *Glamorgan / Llandough* prior to 1950 might now
reside (e.g., regional archives, National Archives holdings, or affiliated
local repository catalogues).

Anyway I anticipate your forgiveness, if I have erred in writing to you
earlier.

Thank you again and in advance for your assistance.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler

FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR ENGAGEMENT

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence, deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process, and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry, archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records as "Mrs Buckler," a misidentification that was never judicially tested and which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings. The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these proceedings-including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of livelihood-to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession. That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100 granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through monastic (1215-1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an 800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological vindication came too late-1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)-yet heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

1.      Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection arising from our family's occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
2.      I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as executive representative and guardian of the Buckler-Williams estate and matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record, restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record pending proper adjudication-which has been historically obstructed through procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined inquiry to animus possidendi (intention to possess) and excluded animus domini (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not ownership rulings-a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

*       Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
*       Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased from records).
*       Unformalized deals like the 1895-1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage protections, incompatible with redevelopment-consequences avoided, raising credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not right with the record:

*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.
*       Land registration before Mary Williams's 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.
*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960-1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).
*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811-1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982-84 library deeds vanishing).
*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543-1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations-covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.

This Notice:

*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.
*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.

Regards, Sion Buckler On behalf of the Buckler-Williams family [address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/ <https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/>

Postscript - Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler's son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.

and record-keeping.

Yours sincerely,


*Sion Buckler*

Councillor Carroll & co,

I write regarding potential gaps in the Council's planning and
record-keeping processes relating to Great House Farm, Llandough, which was
demolished in 1988 following the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler.

Recent evidence suggests the Council may wish to examine its own position
on this matter, as it raises questions about procedural compliance and
record integrity that could expose the authority to wider scrutiny.

CORE ISSUES

**1. Identity and Procedural Integrity**

The 1987 judgment turned on a 1974 licence addressed to "Mrs Buckler". My
grandmother, Mary Williams, did not use or accept this designation.
Contemporaneous evidence (1978 newspaper article attached) records her
asserting ownership under her correct name.

If the 1987 court was not presented with this evidence, the judgment may
rest on an incomplete factual record. This raises procedural fairness
concerns relevant to any future review of the decision.

**2. Heritage Information and Statutory Compliance**

The site's archaeological significance was documented by 1978 (Roman
burials, monastic associations). Yet professional excavations in 1994
revealed 1,026 early medieval burials and monastic structures—findings that
should have prompted evaluation under the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Areas Act 1979.

Critical question: Did the Council conduct or require prior archaeological
assessment before granting permissions to demolish? If not, this represents
a potential gap in statutory process that may affect the validity of the
permissions granted.

**3. Land Registry Disclosure**

BP registered title in 1982 based on the disputed licence. The Council
should establish:
- Whether any dispute notice or heritage caution was lodged;
- Whether the Council disclosed relevant heritage information to the Land
Registry;
- What planning records exist from 1978–1988 regarding the site's known
archaeological potential.

**4. Corporate Identity Inconsistency**

During my father's appeal, the court treated BP Properties Ltd and BP
Pension Trust Ltd inconsistently—as separate entities when convenient, then
as one when dismissing his claim. This raises questions about how
thoroughly the litigation was scrutinised and whether the Council's records
reflect this uncertainty.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE COUNCIL

These issues go beyond a single historical dispute. They touch on:

- **Planning record integrity**: Whether heritage information was
adequately documented and acted upon;
- **Procedural compliance**: Whether statutory protections (Ancient
Monuments Act) were properly applied;
- **Institutional liability**: Whether decisions were made on incomplete or
misleading information;
- **Precedent risk**: Whether similar vulnerabilities may exist in other
historical planning decisions.

REQUESTS

I ask the Council to:

1. **Commission a review** of the planning permissions granted between
1978–1988 for Great House Farm, specifically examining what heritage and
archaeological information was available to decision-makers and how it was
handled.

2. **Refer this matter to the Monitoring Officer** for examination of
procedural compliance and record integrity.

3. **Establish** what correspondence, cautions, or dispute notices exist in
relation to this site's title or heritage status.

4. **Clarify the Council's current protocol** for handling historical title
disputes, previously unknown heritage information, or allegations of
material non-disclosure in past planning processes—to prevent recurrence.

I am not asking the Council to reverse the 1987 judgment or disturb current
residents. I am asking it to ensure its own records are accurate and its
own processes are defensible.

I attach the 1978 article and supporting documents, and am available to
meet or provide further information.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler, Sgt (Ret'd)
Executor for the Manor of Llandough
[address redacted], Dinas Powys, [postcode redacted]

Dear Sion,

The question about archival silences is one upon which there is a voluminous literature. Practically, however, the best way of making sense of what is and is not in the archives is to refer to the reports which shaped selection policies in the modern era - see especially the Report on Departmental Records (Cmnd 9136) and the Report on Legal Records (Cmnd 3084) - and the resulting retention and disposition schedules - see for example the one for the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) published here .

What you will see from these is that the presumption for modern records is against permanent preservation. In general, apart from small samples to demonstrate the ordinary functioning of the courts/government departments, records are only preserved if they bear witness to moments of particular legal or policy significance or change. In the case of legal records, the presumption has been that parties would be responsible for maintaining their own records.

In terms of how to continue your search, my instinct is that you should consider exploring the holdings of the relevant local archive. You can also try some keyword searches in our catalogue - see, for example, these  search results which highlight these  series as potentially a relevant source of desired information. You might also wish to search the registered files of the land registry in records series LAR 1 . You should be advised, however, that departmental records tend to focus more on policy than upon the treatment of individual cases.

*FORMAL NOTICE OF RECORD CHALLENGE, ASSERTION OF RIGHT, AND DEMAND FOR
ENGAGEMENT*

Dear Sir/Madam,

This Notice is issued for placement on official record and for reliance. It
is not informal correspondence. I urge you not to resort to silence,
deflection, or delay, as doing so following receipt of this notice
constitutes knowing reliance upon, and maintenance of, records alleged to
be materially defective through fraud, concealment, denial of due process,
and systemic erasure. Please report any suspicious activity and
discrepancies identified.

This Notice is issued in pursuit of narrative justice at this stage; formal
judicial remedies are expressly reserved. It serves to document our
family's side of the story before it is completely erased and history
rewritten, ensuring awareness among custodians of land, heritage, heraldry,
archaeology, and public records.

My elder brother, Rhys Buckler, and I are the sons of the late William
Buckler (d. 1991), defendant in the landmark legal case *BP Properties Ltd
v Buckler* (1987), and the grandchildren of the late Mary Williams, whose
dispossession, marginalisation, and exclusion from judicial determination
remain unresolved matters of record. Mary Williams was repeatedly and
materially falsely addressed/mislabeled in legal and administrative records
as “Mrs Buckler,” a misidentification that was never judicially tested and
which directly affected the handling, scope, and outcome of proceedings.
The Williams/Buckler family held claim to the land title, having acquired
and occupied Great House Farm continuously since 1667, based on family
records, historical evidence, and centuries of resistance to adverse claims.

I place on record that I am the first member of my family able to speak
publicly and formally on these matters. Other close family members remain
too traumatised and intimidated by the historical conduct of these
proceedings—including violent eviction, demolition, and loss of
livelihood—to engage, despite the continuing consequences of dispossession.
That silence must not be misread as consent, acquiescence, or abandonment
of right. There is a material distinction between free silence and silence
produced by fear, trauma, and coercive experience.

The story, as we have pieced it together, reveals a multi-generational
pattern of lawfare and siege: from Norman/English conquests in 1100
granting lordships over ancient Welsh Christian landscapes, through
monastic (1215–1539) and Crown seizures (1539 onward), to industrial
encroachments (e.g., 1876 Limeworks severance without consent) and modern
corporate possession actions. This culminated in the 1988 demolition of an
800-year-old farmhouse amid police standoffs, leaving the family homeless
and the site scarred, now buried under Church View Close. Archaeological
vindication came too late—1994 excavations revealed over 1,000 Roman and
medieval burials, confirming family warnings (e.g., the 1870 Roman soldier
discovery under the living room floor, suppressed by authorities)—yet
heritage records celebrate the site while omitting our dispossession.

The following assertions of right are now formally placed on record. They
have never been lawfully adjudicated or extinguished:

   1. Rhys Buckler may be the rightful Manorial Lord of the Manor of
   Llandough, by right of primogeniture and continuous hereditary connection
   arising from our family’s occupation of Great House Farm from 1667 until
   our narrative, legal, and physical dispossession.
   2. I assert a claim to act as Squire of the Manor of Llandough, as
   executive representative and guardian of the Buckler–Williams estate and
   matriarchal lineage, with a mandate to pursue correction of record,
   restitution, and restorative remedies.

These are assertions of right, not settled declarations, placed on record
pending proper adjudication—which has been historically obstructed through
procedural narrowing, missing documents, and avoidance of full hearings.

In 1974, Mary Williams was twice prevented from presenting her case and
obtaining a judicial determination of superior ownership, despite claims
grounded in long occupation, intent, and possession. The court confined
inquiry to *animus possidendi* (intention to possess) and excluded *animus
domini* (intention to own), reclassifying her from putative owner to mere
occupier and foreclosing title adjudication. BP sought possession only, not
ownership rulings—a choice unexplained and significant. Proceedings were
adjourned or quashed without resolution.

This occurred despite evidence of ownership intent, including:

   - Centuries-long occupation and resistance (e.g., failed 1938 auction
   due to local support; post-1945 rent disputes).
   - Roman-era remains and historical significance (e.g., Guglielmo
   Marconi's 1897 residence during radio experiments, with family aid erased
   from records).
   - Unformalized deals like the 1895–1905 Daniel Thomas quarrying
   permission for promised title, undermined by vanished deeds.

Judicial ownership examination would have engaged archaeological/heritage
protections, incompatible with redevelopment—consequences avoided, raising
credibility concerns.

Serious unresolved anomalies persist, indicating something is still not
right with the record:

   - Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4
   November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.
   - Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported
   by verifiable coverage.
   - Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title
   determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.
   - Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family
   detriment.
   - Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted
   essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing
   ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).
   - Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches
   ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid
   development).
   - Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert
   Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).
   - Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough
   Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of
   the "battleground" site.

These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation
(e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales'
cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is
illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and
moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but
passage of time does not validate it.

Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment
(absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for
reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.

I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders
(including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs,
historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively,
review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further
rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable
evidence available.

This Notice:

   - Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.
   - Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.
   - Reserves all rights without prejudice.
   - Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may
   aggravate responsibility.

For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.

This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance
becomes untenable.

Regards, Sion Buckler On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [address redacted],
Dinas Powys, Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz

heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a
young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or
differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality
Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability
cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of
ignorance.

Ms Smith,
Thank you for your detailed response regarding selection policies and
retention schedules. I appreciate the procedural clarity you have provided.
However, I must respectfully indicate that your reply does not address the
substantive concerns I have raised, and I am now compelled to escalate this
matter formally.
1. From "Archival Silence" to Potential Evidence Tampering
You correctly note that archival silences are well-documented in academic
literature. However, the circumstances surrounding Great House Farm suggest
something more concerning than routine selection decisions. I am now in
possession of first-hand testimony (David Buckler, 2024) alleging that:

   - Frederick Buckler (my grandfather) and his eldest son engaged a
   solicitor privately in the 1960s
   - Title documents were removed from the family home and allegedly sold
   - The family was deliberately misled with the phrase "it's all been
   dealt with legally"

This testimony, combined with the disappearance of the Bute Estate → Daniel
Thomas deed index card from Cardiff Library (reported missing in 1984),
suggests potential spoliation of evidence rather than routine archival
selection. The question is no longer "why weren't records preserved?" but
"were records deliberately removed to prejudice a 320-year possessory
claim?"
2. The Computerised Records Question
You direct me to search your catalogue. I have done so. However, I now ask
specifically:

   - Does The National Archives hold any digitised or microfilmed copies of
   the Bute Estate records that might contain references to the Daniel
   Thomas quarrying agreement (circa 1895-1905) or the 1938 auction at the
   Bear Hotel?
   - Are there any internal indices or finding aids (particularly from the
   1970s-1980s) that might reference Great House Farm, Llandough, or the
   BP/Western Ground Rents acquisition records that are not reflected in the
   current online catalogue?

The 1994 archaeological excavation report (Cotswold Archaeological Trust)
confirms the site's national significance. The absence of corresponding
land transaction records from the same period is itself an anomaly
requiring explanation.
3. The BP Corporate Records Question
You note that parties are generally responsible for maintaining their own
records. However, BP Properties Ltd and BP Pension Trust Ltd were corporate
entities with statutory filing obligations. I ask:

   - Were any BP corporate records relating to land acquisition in South
   Glamorgan (1969-1988) selected for preservation under the Companies Act
   or as part of the public record?
   - Has The National Archives ever received or sought records from BP
   regarding the Great House Farm acquisition, demolition, or the 1987
   litigation?

The Court of Appeal judgment [1987] EWCA Civ 2 notes that BP issued letters
on 31 October 1974, not received until November 4th 1974 —letters that were
allegedly "accepted by silence." The original correspondence would
constitute primary evidence of potentially fraudulent misrepresentation. If
these were not preserved, I ask under what authority they were destroyed
and whether this occurred before or after the litigation concluded.
4. Request for Formal Investigation
I am not seeking annotation of records. I am seeking:

   1. A formal review of whether records relating to Great House Farm,
   Llandough (ST 168 733) were selected for preservation, destroyed, or
   remain non accessioned;
   2. A search of microfilm, digitised, or legacy finding aid holdings for
   any reference to the 1938 auction, Western Ground Rents acquisition, or the
   Daniel Thomas quarrying agreement;
   3. Confirmation of whether The National Archives has ever received
   complaints regarding missing Bute Estate records or BP land acquisition
   documents from other researchers;
   4. Guidance on the appropriate authority to investigate allegations of
   document removal from Cardiff Library (1984) and potential fraud in the
   1982 land registration.

5. Public Interest and Parliamentary Scrutiny
This matter involves:

   - The forced removal of a family from land occupied since at least 1667
   - Demolition of a medieval structure described as a "dilapidated utility
   building" to avoid heritage protection
   - Archaeological discoveries (1888, 1994) that were known but officially
   "forgotten"
   - A Court of Appeal decision ([1987] EWCA Civ 2) that may have relied on
   incomplete or fraudulent evidence

I am copying my MP and the Parliamentary Ombudsman in this correspondence.
I will also be submitting a Subject Access Request to HM Land Registry
regarding the 1982 registration and a complaint to the Information
Commissioner's Office regarding potential destruction of records relevant
to ongoing property disputes.
I request a substantive response addressing the specific questions above
within 20 working days. Should The National Archives be unable to assist
further, I request a formal referral to the appropriate body with
jurisdiction over historical record fraud and spoliation.
Yours sincerely,
Sion Buckler

Ms Smith,

Thanks for your reply and for explaining The National Archives’ position
regarding annotation and review of records.

I fully accept that archives do not resolve disputes and that records are
often incomplete or patchwork in character. My purpose in writing is not to
seek amendment, adjudication, or retrospective commentary, but to raise a
specific concern about how absence, silence, and fragmentation within the
archival record should be understood where material public consequences
clearly followed.

By way of clarification, my concern relates to the historical record
surrounding Great House Farm, Llandough, and the proceedings culminating in *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2. In particular:

   - Ownership and occupation of the farmhouse and garden were actively
   contested in 1974, with a defence asserting adverse possession filed on
   behalf of Mary Williams, and the matter adjourned without a final
   determination of title.
   - Enforcement of earlier possession orders was deferred, a warrant was
   withdrawn on 31 October 1974, and the occupier remained in possession until
   her death in 1983.
   - Despite this, land registration, demolition (1988), and archaeological
   intervention proceeded without a High Court determination of ownership and
   without disclosure of earlier, locally known archaeological discoveries.
   - A Roman burial reportedly discovered beneath the farmhouse in 1888 by
   the occupying family appears not to have been reflected in later “rescue”
   excavations (1978–1980) or the major 1994 excavation, which treated Roman
   and early medieval burials as newly revealed.

Taken together, this produces an archival landscape in which:

   - court files relating to decisive events appear absent or incomplete;
   - later records imply finality where proceedings were in fact unresolved;
   - and the destruction of a long-occupied medieval structure occurred
   before the site’s known archaeological significance was formally
   acknowledged.

I note and appreciate your confirmation that the principal judicial series
(J 157, J 83, J 84) contain no relevant material. Given the scale of the
consequences flowing from the dispute—forced removal, demolition of an
occupied dwelling, and loss of heritage fabric—the absence of supporting
court or administrative files is itself significant for researchers.

Accordingly, I would be grateful for guidance on the following procedural
points:

   - how researchers are expected to interpret gaps or silence in the
   archival record where substantial actions plainly occurred;
   - whether related non-judicial records (for example, departmental,
   planning, regulatory, or corporate records connected to land registration,
   planning consent, or archaeological works) are more likely to sit outside
   the obvious court series; and
   - whether there is an appropriate mechanism for flagging concerns about
   record completeness or contextual risk, without seeking alteration of the
   records themselves.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging impropriety on the part of
The National Archives or its staff. My concern is to ensure that the
historical record is approached with appropriate caution where absence may
unintentionally convey certainty or closure that did not exist at the time.

Thank you again for your time and professionalism.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Ms Taylor,

Thanks for your reply and for outlining the options available to consult
the estate plans referenced.

I should clarify my position, as my correspondence is not a routine request
for private research access, but part of a wider and serious concern
regarding possible historical misdescription, suppression, and/or
concealment of material facts relating to Great House Farm, Llandough.

I am currently at the Welsh settlement in Argentina, having been displaced
from my ancestral birthplace in Llandough. As such, it is not possible for
me to attend the searchroom in person so easy as you're 7,500 miles away,
nor to “pop in” to consult records on site. Requiring physical attendance
or payment for access is therefore not a practical or equitable option in
my circumstances.

More importantly, my concern is that certain archival descriptions,
surveys, and planning-era records may themselves be inaccurate or
incomplete as a result of earlier failures of disclosure. Specifically, a
Roman burial reportedly discovered at Great House Farm in 1888 appears to
have been treated as a “surprise” in later archaeological surveys
(1978/1994), and an occupied, c.800-year-old domestic dwelling was
repeatedly described in planning documentation as an “old barn” or “utility
building.” These characterisations materially affected heritage protection,
culminating in demolition in 1988.

In that context, I am not seeking to pay for copies of records whose
accuracy is itself in question, nor to participate financially in processes
that may inadvertently perpetuate errors arising from that period. My
intention is to place relevant public bodies on notice of a potential issue
of public record integrity and heritage governance, not to obtain documents
for private interest. I have written to the Senedd calling for a public
enquiry too. I've notified the land registry and serious fraud teams too.

I am therefore asking that my correspondence be treated as a formal
expression of concern regarding the reliability and completeness of the
archival record as it relates to this site, and that this concern be noted
accordingly. I would also be grateful if you could advise which department
or officer is appropriate for addressing concerns of this nature, where the
issue is not access but potential historical misrepresentation within
public records.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not alleging any impropriety on the part
of current archive staff. My concern relates to historical processes and
decisions, and to ensuring that those matters are properly examined rather
than inadvertently reinforced.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for clarifying the nature of your enquiry.

In answer to your main enquiry, in general we would not add notes to, or review, records in light of unresolved disputes or other matters. The records are left to speak for themselves. In fact, those records are often incomplete and patchwork in character, meaning that they may not enable the enquirer to know what the final determination or outcome of any dispute was.

Since you refer to a reported Court of Appeal (Civil Division) case, I have conducted a quick search of our, admittedly limited holdings. The main record series in which you might expect to find archival material here are J 157<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C9764>, J 83<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C9691> and J 84<https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C9692>. Unfortunately, none contain records relevant to the case.

Yours sincerely,

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for contacting The National Archives of the United Kingdom.

It is unlikely The National Archives holds the records of this type of case, and the Central Land Registry , who hold records of land registration, is a separate body. Some records of land ownership can be found among records at local or county archives.

I recommend you consult our guide to searching for records of Land ownership records and deeds: an overview - The National Archives . Regarding the court cases you mention, I also recommend you consult: Civil court cases: Chancery Division since 1875 - The National Archives , and you may also find Civil courts: appeal cases after 1875 - The National Archives  of use to your research. These guides will help you to use our catalogue , or other online sources, effectively and focus your search.

Records are represented in our online catalogue by a title, a reference and a brief description. When you search our catalogue using keywords you are searching across these titles and descriptions, rather than the contents of the records themselves. By clicking on any search result, you can see whether the record is available online or if you need to visit us to view the original. You can also request copies of records from their catalogue description page.

If the record is held by another archive, you will need to contact them directly to find out how you can access it.

You can also watch this video  for more advice on using our online catalogue.

You are welcome to visit us  to continue your research here in person, where access to our records is free of charge. Before you visit, please check our website for information regarding our opening hours  and ID requirements . If you are unable to visit, or would like someone to pursue this research on your behalf, please see the available paid search options  on our website.

Yours sincerely,

Robert Fleming﻿

Remote Enquiries Duty Officer
www.nationalarchives.gov.uk

Individual cases
In line with the general practice of select committees, the Committee is unable to take up individual cases, including those relating to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO). The Committee is responsible for scrutinising the general work and performance of the PHSO, and to examine any reports it lays before Parliament, but it does not have any power to compel or direct the Ombudsman to act in a particular way.
The Committee cannot review the PHSO's decisions about individual cases. This includes the PHSO's decisions on whether or not to accept a case. As the office of the PHSO is independent, decisions cannot be overruled by a government minister or any parliamentary committee.
However, if you are not happy with a PHSO decision, you can ask the PHSO to review that decision. Proposals for scrutiny work and meeting requests
While we welcome proposals for future inquiries and scrutiny work, we cannot comment on the potential merits or likelihood of implementation of such suggestions. The Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) is appointed by the House of Commons to examine: constitutional issues; the quality and standards of administration provided by Civil Service departments; and the reports of the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO).

Subject: Systemic governance concern regarding historic land registration and administrative reliance - BP vs Buckler 1987 (inc. BP Land Registry 1982)


Dear Committee Members,

I am writing to draw your attention to a historical land matter which I believe may illustrate potential vulnerabilities in public administration, record-keeping, and the governance of land registration. My purpose is solely to provide factual information for consideration, rather than to request remedial action.

The matter concerns land formerly known as Great House Farm, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan, later developed for residential use and historically associated with BP v Buckler (Court of Appeal, 1987).

Chronology of relevant events (as reflected in public records):

  *   July 1974: Court proceedings involving my grandmother were adjourned without determination of ownership.
  *   31 October 1974: A subsequent hearing did not proceed substantively, following correspondence received from BP entities that same day. No judgment on ownership was issued.
  *   Throughout this period, my grandmother was not included in dealings concerning the land, while the opposing party continued to assert ownership.
  *   1982: The land was registered in the name of BP entities, despite unresolved competing claims and no final judicial adjudication.
  *   1983: My grandmother passed away after the registration, with ownership never conclusively adjudicated.
  *   1987 Court of Appeal: The record reflects an apparent inconsistency in the treatment of correspondence and corporate entities. Specifically:

     *   The court noted that my grandmother had replied to correspondence on 31 October, asserting ownership.
     *   The reply was treated as directed to the “wrong” corporation (BP Pensions Trust Ltd rather than BP Properties Ltd).
     *   In a later appeal by my father, the same judge acknowledged that both BP entities were effectively treated as the same for the purposes of the ruling.
     *   These circumstances resulted in the court upholding the opposing party’s registration despite prior correspondence demonstrating an assertion of ownership.

  *   Following these proceedings, my father’s application to the European Court of Human Rights was blocked.
  *   The family home was demolished, preventing re-entry, even for the retrieval of personal belongings.
  *   Despite its historical significance and a petition to protect it, the property was not preserved. The house had prior heritage interest, including documented connections to Marconi.
  *   1991: My father passed away at just 41.
  *   1994: The land was subsequently excavated, with items of archaeological interest removed.

Taken together, these events demonstrate a situation in which land registration and subsequent reliance by public bodies proceeded without definitive adjudication of ownership, raising questions regarding administrative safeguards, procedural coherence, and record integrity.

I am submitting this information purely for institutional awareness. I am not making allegations of misconduct, nor requesting investigation. I am able to provide a concise factual timeline and references to public records should it assist the Committee’s understanding.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
